Maladaptive Strategies.value: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

vignette: When Ahmed first sat across the table, the rain against the window seemed to echo the hollow silence of a memory he could not quite contain. He told the story of that night in the old townhouse where his former partner, Layla, had pushed him to the floor of the basement, her fist striking his ribs as the hallway lights flickered out. The darkness, the claustrophobic physical location, and the distant whine of a helicopter over the city’s airport—an echo of the same metallic roar he heard at night—had become impossible triggers that, whenever they surfaced, flooded his mind with the raw sound of Layla’s cry and the taste of blood. The sudden darkness and the helicopter’s hum pulled him back to that basement, a place where he could not escape the memory. Ahmed’s sense of betrayal, that someone he had trusted could become the source of such violence, seeded a belief that he had somehow been doomed by his own character. He came to think that the abuse happened because he was a “weak” person, that his own flaws had invited Layla’s cruelty. That sense of being fundamentally flawed fed directly into how he recalled the night. Every time he tried to revisit the scene, the recollection was a series of disjointed fragments—one moment the weight of the floorboard under his fingers, the next the sharp smell of sweat—yet the core of it was always wrapped in the accusation that he had somehow brought it upon himself. The conviction that he was fundamentally untrustworthy and that the world was a place where betrayal was inevitable magnified the intensity of his triggers. Even a simple flicker of a streetlight or the hiss of a traffic signal could remind him of the basement’s oppressive gloom. The knowledge that “people” could turn on him made the mere presence of other humans feel like a looming threat, turning ordinary social settings into arenas of potential danger. The night’s memory began to dictate Ahmed’s coping strategies. He could no longer walk into a dimly lit community hall without pausing, listening for the sound of a helicopter or the echo of a stairwell. His new routine involved wearing a long, dark jacket, covering his shoulders so that no one could see him moving. He stayed behind the counter when community meetings were held, glancing over his shoulder for anyone he deemed suspicious. The feeling that every shadow might conceal an assailant became so entrenched that his own safety plans relied on vigilance and concealment. Each time Ahmed forced himself to recall the night, the negative appraisals he held—betrayal, self-blame, shattered worldviews—were reaffirmed. The memory acted as a mirror, reflecting back his belief that he had been wronged by a partner who had turned on him and that the world was a place that would always conspire to harm him. The more he thought about the event, the deeper he sank into the conviction that his own character made him vulnerable to such harm, and the more his sense of personal agency diminished. The vivid auditory details of the night—Layla’s labored breathing, the clatter of a dropped object—were not merely recollections but triggers that, without warning, would strike him in a crowded street or when a helicopter’s rotors cut across the sky. One afternoon, as he walked to a local park to attend a community outreach session, a helicopter’s roar broke his concentration and suddenly he was back in the basement, hearing the floor creak and his heart pound. Those unanticipated spikes in arousal served to deepen his avoidance of light, sound, and places that echoed his past trauma. Ahmed’s avoidance and hypervigilance fed back into his negative appraisals. By constantly staying on edge, he could not see any evidence that people were trustworthy or that he could protect himself without extreme measures. The belief that he was at risk of betrayal hardened into a rationalization for his continued secrecy and guardedness. In his mind, the only way to keep himself safe was to remain unseen, to keep others from seeing him as a potential target. This protective logic only strengthened his conviction that the world was unforgiving. Finally, the very strategies Ahmed employed—staying hidden in the dark, keeping his movements deliberate, and watching for any potential danger—only amplified his triggers. When he avoided the basement of the old townhouse, he found himself turning his back on the building and avoiding the stairwell of the community center where volunteers gathered. Even the dark corners of the town hall, where he had once organized meetings, became sites of anxiety, making him retreat further into the periphery. Each avoidance reinforced the belief that certain places were inherently unsafe, solidifying the cycle of hypervigilance and fear. It is this compulsion to avoid, to conceal, and to remain on guard that has finally led Ahmed to seek help. After months of feeling exhausted, isolated, and terrified at the slightest rumble of a helicopter or a dim streetlamp, he realized that his life was being dictated by a single night in a basement. He fears that if he does not change his current pattern, he will lose his role as a community organizer, his ability to connect with others, and ultimately his sense of identity. Yet, deep down, he hopes that confronting the memory and the associated beliefs might allow him to reclaim the safety he once felt in the dark corners of his community.
